notes: Tollmere's binder. Sells the four beginners' tomes and a shelf of Vale books; buys books. Her view of the Circle is the outsider's view of it, which is the only unflattering one in the pack.

greetings.text: Four hundred and forty copies, and the Row reads the stone aloud in the taverns, badly, with feeling. The Guild sent back its ribbon. I have framed the ribbon.
The Guild paid on the nail and locked it in a drawer. My copy is on the back of an invoice, in a box under the press. One day somebody will want it. I will be here.
The third line means what it says, the Woodfolk tell me. I have sold six copies of that sentence already. Nobody knows what it means. That is why they buy it.
You have been Calling. Don't look like that; it gets into the hands. You've the same grip on the door that the old ones have, like you're not sure the room will be there.
The famous one. I'll not make a fuss. I will say that two people came in this month asking whether I'd a book about you, and I said give it a year.
A Listener. Then you'll want the First Lecture, and you'll want it in the cheap binding, because you'll be writing in it inside a week whatever you promise Sulion.
I've heard. Your marks are the same colour as anybody's, and I'd like you to keep your hands where the paste isn't.

q_the_stride_dedication_offer.speaker: Cassa Binder
q_the_stride_dedication_offer.text: I want the words. A rubbing is how you get words off a stone without the stone. — A rafter told me, over a book he could not read and bought anyway, that the half-cut block in the Old Quarry in the Wold has Oroth on its hidden face: the Stride's own dedication, cut and never laid. The Guild will hear of it the same way I did, and the Guild has a use for good granite, which is doorsteps. — Take paper and charcoal. The weavers like the cut face. I am told they do not like charcoal, which is not the same thing as being frightened of it.

q_the_stride_dedication_accept.speaker: Cassa Binder
q_the_stride_dedication_accept.text: Do not fold it. — I will know. A fold in a rubbing is a lie told in the grain, and I do not bind lies unless somebody pays me extra and signs for it.

q_the_stride_dedication_decide_print_it.speaker: Cassa Binder
q_the_stride_dedication_decide_print_it.text: Forty to the Spire and four hundred to the Row, and one to the Guild, gratis, with a ribbon. — I will put your name in the front. No? Then I will put 'a walker', which is what the stone says, more or less.

q_the_stride_dedication_decide_sell_to_t.speaker: Cassa Binder
q_the_stride_dedication_decide_sell_to_t.text: To the Guild. — I will do it, because I said I would do what you said, and I will copy it out first in my own hand on the back of an invoice, because I am a binder and not a saint.

q_the_stride_dedication_decide_to_the_wo.speaker: Cassa Binder
q_the_stride_dedication_decide_to_the_wo.text: The Woodfolk. — Nobody in this city has ever asked them anything. Go on, then. Take it to Elderhold. Tell them a bookbinder sends her compliments and would like to know what the third line means, if they do.

q_the_stride_dedication_decide.speaker: Cassa Binder
q_the_stride_dedication_decide.text: Two hundred and six. The Guild has been counting wrong for four hundred years and charging by the count. — I could bind this in a week and sell forty copies to the Spire and four hundred to the Row, and the Guild would never forgive me, and I would sleep like a child. Or not. It is your rubbing. You walked into the Wold for it.

choices.text: Bind it. Sell it. Let the city read it.
Take it back to the Wold. It's their stone.

greet.speaker: Cassa Binder
greet.text: Mind the boards, they're wet. Books on the shelf, tomes in the press, and anything on the bench is somebody else's and not for sale no matter what you offer.

choices.text: What do you make of the Circle?
Does anybody buy the Vale books?
Would you buy a book from me?
The Guild's entry for the Lantern Row strongroom.
The block in the Old Quarry. You want a rubbing.
Two hundred and six lamps. The last stone isn't laid.

trade.speaker: Cassa Binder
trade.text: Kindle-Bolt, Hush-Frost, Ward and Quiet the Blood: the four the Spire sends them down the hill for, and I keep them in that order because that is the order they come asking. The rest of what I have is Vale reading, and the primer, which sells more than all of it together because every child in this city has to be got through Naming Day somehow.

the_tomes.speaker: Cassa Binder
the_tomes.text: I sell the working written down. That is not the same thing and I say so to everyone who asks, because one day somebody is going to buy Raise the Buried off me, take it out to a hedge, do exactly what it says, and be very surprised. — A tome is somebody's hands, written out by somebody else's. You read it, and then you go and do it badly for a month, and then it is yours. Anyone who tells you the book did it is selling you a second book.

the_circle.speaker: Cassa Binder
the_circle.text: Three people who disagree, and me, and I have copied out all three of them by hand, which is a closer reading than any of them have given the other two. — Sulion is right about more of it and insufferable about all of it. Cresswell is wrong and kind, which wears better than it should. Ondrael is honest, and honesty in a Sayer reads as weakness to the other two, and they are both a little afraid of her anyway. Three hundred years of that. I have the ledgers; the arguments get shorter and the bindings get cheaper.

the_vale_books.speaker: Cassa Binder
the_vale_books.text: The cookery, always. The bestiary, to men who intend to go out on the downs and would rather be lied to first. The play, in spring, when the Long Table's coming and everybody wants to be the one who knows the extra stanza. — And the Candle Book, which nobody buys. They come in and read a page of it standing up and put it back and go home to their grandmother's copy. I keep two on the shelf for that exact purpose and I have never sold one in nine years.

the_strongroom_entry.speaker: Cassa Binder
the_strongroom_entry.text: Nine hundred and ninety-eight, the eleventh month. Four leaves. — I have copied that entry eleven times in nine years: for clerks, for a Sayer, and twice for men who did not give a reason and paid in old marks. Two sheets of paper and the sitting, which is six, and you may have it in the cheap wrapper because you will be carrying it somewhere wet, everybody who wants that entry is going somewhere wet.

choices.text: Eleven times and nobody has asked you the question?

the_fourth_wall.speaker: Cassa Binder
the_fourth_wall.text: Not once, and I have waited, and I am going to say it to you for nothing because nine years is long enough. — Three walls of coursed limestone and a fourth they did not build. Fused black stone. Curved. Of no known thickness. Eleven feet down at the foot of Lantern Row, and the mason said he would strike the black stone at eleven and did, and the Guild wrote it up as a saving. — There is one curved black Builder thing under that end of this city and it is not a wall. I have set it down at the foot of my own copy in my own hand and nobody has ever read the foot of the last leaf, which tells you everything about clerks.

buying.speaker: Cassa Binder
buying.text: I will, if it is a book and not a wet thing you pulled out of a barrow. I smell the spine. That is not a superstition: a book that has been under ground has a smell, and it goes into everything on the shelf beside it, and then I am selling ruined stock to people who trusted me. Twice I have handed one back across this counter and both times the man went away angry and both times I was right.
